catalog_quote: Kukuya is a tonal language and the tone patterns can encode lexical and grammatical distinctions. What is of particular interest here is the fact that in Kukuya there are five fixed tonal melodies which are L, H, LH, HL and LHL. ... In addition, a stem-initial prominence interacts with the tonal system as well as the phonetic realisation of consonants and vowels. [p. 33] ... In this subsection I describe this interesting phenomenon in Kukuya, which is labeled as the “positional prominence” or “stem-initial accent” (Hyman 2007, 2015; Lionnet 2017). Here I adopt the term “accent” and refer it to an abstract property that can influence the licensing potential of consonants and vowels as well as the realisation of tone patterns. [p. 45] ... the domain-initial tone is always immutable: it is never affected by any tone that occurs to its left or right; ... the vowel reduction operates on V2 which is an immediately post-accentual unaccentuated mora, such that /a/ in this position is often realised as a schwa, which is also similar to that typically found in stress languages; [p. 46] ... Like in many other Northwest Bantu languages, there is always a stem-initial accent delimiting the left boundary of a prosodic domain in Kukuya, which reflects the phonological strengthening of the accented material, both segmentally and tonally. [p. 48]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Teke-Kukuya is not in the catalog; this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Hyman 1987 'Prosodic domains in Kukuya' (NLLT 5: 311–333, DOI 10.1007/BF00134552). It is closed access everywhere checked (Unpaywall, OpenAlex, OpenAIRE, Semantic Scholar, Springer paywall with no abstract, absent from Hyman's Berkeley page; archive. Every citing context found uses it for tone (five stem melodies on the prosodic stem, prepausal stem-H lowering at p. 318, prefix + preceding stem forming a clitic-group-like domain), so it is prosody-but-not-word-stress; medium priority to obtain because it may repeat Paulian's accent claim. Four open Hyman papers were downloaded from his Berkeley page and. The best stress statement actually read is Hyman 2008 (Linguistics 46: 333–334), reporting that Paulian 1975 analyses Kukuya as having a stem-initial accent (pause before every stem-initial C, gemination of stem-initial nasals/l, prefixes cliticise leftward), corroborated by Hyman 2013: 317 listing Kukuya under 'initial' (= stem-initial) accent placement in NW Bantu. Paulian 1975 itself remains print-only (HathiTrust search-only; Harvard offsite) and is the high-value acquisition for a first-hand statement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kukuya is a tone language (five stem melodies L, H, LH, HL, LHL). Its only accent-like prominence is a fixed stem-initial (root-initial) accent: the first syllable/mora of every stem is prominent - full consonant inventory and aspiration only there, initial m/n/l geminated, a slight pause before other initial consonants, immutable tone on the initial mora, post-accentual vowel reduction (a > schwa in V2). Noun-class, concord and subject prefixes are unaccented and are not part of the stem's domain; they cliticise to the PRECEDING stem, so the prosodic domain is stem + following prefix(es) and the accent falls on its left edge. No penultimate or word-final prominence is described.
new_statements.exceptions: The one exception noted to the immutability of the accented initial mora is the utterance-final lowering rule, which also affects the initial mora of an underlying-H stem (p. 46). Prefixes are never accented (p. 47). Prominence is called an 'abstract property' (positional prominence), not phonetic stress; Li states her phonology relies heavily on Paulian (1975) and Hyman (1987), though she did her own fieldwork.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic stem / postlexical prosodic domain (stem + following prefixes across the word boundary), not the grammatical word (prefix + stem); statement applies to nominal and verbal stems generally, not only citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Li 2024 describes the Kukuya variety of Teke spoken on the Kukuya plateau (Lékana / Djambala area, Republic of Congo), the same variety Paulian 1975 recorded in Brazzaville, Lagué, Ngoulonkila and Lékana; this matches Glottolog teke1280 / ISO kkw (Teke-Kukuya). Other Teke varieties (Teke-Tege, Teke-Tsaayi, Teke-Fuumu, etc.) are separate glottocodes and are not covered by this statement.

new_statements.quote: Paulian (1975) has interpreted similar facts as evidence of a stem-initial accent in Kukuya, another NWB language. [...] Even more important are three additional properties pointed out by Paulian (1975): (i) there is a ''pause'', however slight, before every C1 consonant (ii) a C1 nasal or /l/ is automatically geminated (/PùAnónó/ → [b.nnɔ́.nɔ́] ''selfishness'') (iii) prefixes join the preceding stem to form a clitic-group-like P-domain. Paulian takes all of the above properties — especially (i) and (ii) — to be indications of a stem-initial accent in Kukuya.

Linguistics 46(2): 309–350, at pp. 333–334 (reporting Paulian, Christiane 1975, Le kukuya, langue teke du Congo: phonologie, classes nominales. Paris: SELAF).
new_statements.locator: §5.1, p. 333 (PDF page 25), text around example (42) and properties (i)–(iii); continued p. 334
new_statements.reading: Kukuya is a tone language (five stem tone melodies L, H, LH, HL, LHL) whose only dedicated phonological description, Paulian 1975, posits a demarcative STEM-INITIAL ACCENT: prominence falls on the first syllable of the stem (root), diagnosed by a slight pause before the stem-initial consonant, automatic gemination of stem-initial nasals and /l/, and leftward cliticisation of noun-class prefixes onto the preceding stem. Hyman 2013: 317 independently lists Kukuya under 'initial' accent placement (NW Bantu type) and notes that 'initial' there means stem-initial. Caveats: this is Hyman's second-hand report of Paulian, not Paulian's own wording (Paulian 1975 is print-only / HathiTrust search-only; Harvard Widener Library (offsite storage), Philol 894 vol.49-50), and the 'accent' is a phonetic/demarcative stem-edge prominence in a tonal system rather than a lexical stress contrast. If coded, the language would be fixed stem-initial (initial on the prosodic stem, prefixes excluded), tone-bearing.

sources.quote: An additional question concerns the relation of PL to accentual prominence (stress). There are three common claims concerning accent placement in Bantu: (16) a. initial — mostly NW Bantu; e.g. Duala, Kukuya, Bobangi, Ntomba, Bolia, Tetela b. penult — mostly Eastern and Southern Bantu (examples above) c. none — scattered, probably widespread; e.g. Mongo [...] In fact, initial and penultimate accent are not parallel. Initial usually means stem initial, as in Ntomba
